name: Margaret Murray
specialization: Witch-cult hypothesis; anthropological interpretation of witch trial records as evidence for pre-Christian religion

major_works.title: The Witch-Cult in Western Europe
major_works.significance: Argued that witch trials prosecuted a real surviving pre-Christian fertility cult; enormously influential despite being thoroughly discredited; shaped popular witchcraft imagination and Wicca

major_works.title: The God of the Witches
major_works.significance: Popular extension of the witch-cult thesis; more accessible version reaching wide audience

major_works.title: The Divine King in England
major_works.significance: Extension of ritual-sacrifice theory to English monarchy; further demonstration of her anthropological method applied to historical sources

core_argument: Witch trials prosecuted real members of an organized pre-Christian fertility cult worshipping a horned god, which had survived underground through the medieval period. Confessions extracted under torture reflected actual cult practices, not delusion or judicial coercion. This 'Dianic cult' had organized covens, sabbath meetings, and a consistent theology across Western Europe.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Witch trial confessions from across Western Europe, selected and interpreted to support cult-survival hypothesis
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Consistency of confession content as evidence for real underlying practices
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Selective reading of confessional testimony; anthropological analogy with other documented folk religions

key_contributions.claim: A real pre-Christian fertility cult survived into the early modern period; witch trials were persecution of genuine religious practitioners
key_contributions.implication: If true (it is not), would require complete reinterpretation of trial evidence as religious history rather than judicial history

key_contributions.claim: Murray's thesis was adopted by Gerald Gardner as the historical basis for Wicca in the 1950s; whether Murray believed this application is unclear
key_contributions.implication: Her work has had enormous cultural influence despite scholarly rejection

key_contributions.claim: The persistence of Murray's influence (Encyclopedia Britannica carried her thesis as credible until 1968) demonstrates how historical mythologies can outlast their debunking
key_contributions.implication: Murray's thesis is now primarily significant as a study in how false historical narratives achieve and maintain cultural authority

reception_and_critique.major_influences: James George Frazer (Golden Bough), evolutionary anthropology, Egyptological methodology
criticisms: Norman Cohn (Europe's Inner Demons, 1975) systematically demolished the thesis showing Murray misquoted, truncated, and selectively used sources
No independent evidence for a organized pan-European fertility cult exists
Confessions were produced by torture and leading questions, not free testimony about real practices
The 'consistency' of confessions reflects shared demonological questioning procedures, not shared cult practices
Hutton's Triumph of the Moon (1999) provided definitive debunking while sympathetically explaining why the thesis was compelling

historiographical_significance: Murray's witch-cult thesis is the most influential false thesis in witchcraft historiography. Accepted by major reference works and academic figures for decades, it shaped popular witchcraft belief, gave historical legitimacy to Wicca, and required sustained scholarly effort to dislodge. As a historiographical case study, it illustrates how authority, selectivity, and cultural need can sustain a false thesis; and how thorough debunking (Cohn, Hutton) is required to clear the field for rigorous analysis.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
